[h2]Grand Theft Auto V Steam Review[/h2]
[b]Rating:[/b] 🟢 [b]Recommended[/b]

[h3]The Ultimate Nostalgia Trip, But Make It 60 FPS[/h3]
If you had told me back in 2013, huddled over a humming, overheating PlayStation 3 with the original dualshock clacking away, that I would one day be cruising down the Vinewood Hills at a buttery-smooth 60 frames per second on Steam, I probably would have cried.

Back on the PS3, GTA V was a technical marvel. We all stared in awe at the sun setting over Los Santos, forgiving the occasional texture pop-in, the 30 FPS drops during massive explosions, and the agonizingly long loading screens where you could easily go make a sandwich while Trevor was loading in. It was a masterpiece of its generation.

Fast forward to playing it on Steam, and it feels like meeting an old friend who just got a massive glow-up.

[h3]What’s Better on Steam?[/h3]
[list]
[] [b]Performance & Fidelity:[/b] Going from the console versions of the past to a modern PC setup is night and day. The draw distances, the crisp 1080p/4K resolution, and the fluid frame rates breathe entirely new life into a world I thought I knew by heart.
[] [b]Mods & Customization:[/b] While the vanilla game is fantastic, the PC modding community is the real MVP. Whether it's graphical overhauls, quality-of-life tweaks, or just messing around, it adds endless replay value.
[*] [b]Seamless Convenience:[/b] Having it right in your Steam library alongside your achievements, screenshots, and friends list makes jumping back into Los Santos effortless.
[/list]

[h3]The Verdict[/h3]
Coming back to this game after years away feels weirdly comforting. Sure, the radio ads are permanently burned into my brain, and I can still navigate the map blindfolded, but the charm hasn't faded one bit. Michael, Franklin, and Trevor are just as chaotic and entertaining as they were a decade ago.

If you’re on the fence about double-dipping or jumping over from the old console days, do it. It’s a nostalgic masterpiece that still holds its own, and experiencing it without the hardware limitations of 2013 is the ultimate way to play.

Grand Theft Auto V is not just a video game; it is a monumental cultural phenomenon and a sprawling, technicolor mirror held up to the face of modern capitalism. From the moment you step into the sun-drenched, smog-choked streets of Los Santos, Rockstar Games delivers a masterclass in open-world design, storytelling, and social commentary. It captures the chaotic essence of the American Dream, chews it up, and spits it back out in a glorious explosion of high-speed chases, bullet-riddled bank heists, and dark, unfiltered humor.
At the beating heart of this epic narrative is the franchise’s most ambitious storytelling mechanic: the three-protagonist system. By weaving together the lives of three distinct criminals, the game offers a multi-layered perspective of a deeply flawed world. There is Michael, a retired bank robber trapped in a toxic, wealthy suburban nightmare, suffocated by the boredom of his own success. Then there is Franklin, a young, ambitious street hustler trying to escape the cycle of the ghetto by climbing the ladder of organized crime. And finally, Trevor, a volatile, unhinged, and borderline psychotic meth-dealer who embodies the absolute, chaotic id of the GTA franchise itself. The ability to seamlessly switch between these characters creates a dynamic, cinematic rhythm where a tranquil day at a luxury mansion can instantly dissolve into a chaotic desert shootout.
The true star of the show, however, is the map of San Andreas itself. The attention to detail is staggering. Los Santos feels alive, reacting dynamically to the player's presence. Pedestrians yell on their cell phones, traffic clogs the freeways at rush hour, and the neon lights of Vinewood reflect beautifully off the hoods of stolen supercars. Whether you are planning a meticulously detailed, multi-stage heist, diving into the ocean depths, hijacking a military fighter jet, or simply driving down Del Perro Beach while listening to a satirical talk-radio station, the level of player freedom remains completely unmatched.
Ultimately, Grand Theft Auto V stands as a timeless masterpiece because it doesn’t just let you play in a world; it forces you to experience its madness. It is a brilliant, cynical, and wildly entertaining critique of celebrity culture, government corruption, and consumerism. Decades from now, when historians look back at how video games evolved into the definitive art form of the 21st century, GTA V will undoubtedly stand tall as the pinnacle of interactive entertainment.

Title: A Masterpiece… but Missing One Simple Freedom

Baldur’s Gate 3 is easily one of the best RPGs ever made.
The world is rich, the characters are unforgettable, and the amount of freedom in quests and combat is incredible. Every fight feels tactical, every choice matters, and the replay value is huge. It’s a game that pulls you in and refuses to let go.

But there is one major limitation that holds it back for players like me:
you cannot freely customise your own full party.

For a game that celebrates freedom, it’s surprising that creating a full custom team is restricted. Many players enjoy building their own party of heroes — not because we dislike the companions, but because we love tactical synergy, role‑playing, and experimenting with different builds. Even creating just three custom characters makes the game harder, because the difficulty doesn’t scale down.

It feels like the game pushes you toward using Origin companions, even when you want to enjoy the story your own way.

Still, despite this limitation, BG3 remains an amazing experience.
The writing, combat, music, and world-building are top-tier.
I just hope that one day, Larian gives players the option to create a full custom party without workarounds.

A game this good deserves that extra freedom.

Let's start with the character creator. Your options are: burly man or petite sexy woman. There are more options for sexy woman than burly man. I came in wanting to make a butch woman, like my character in the TTRPG.  No. You cannot make butch, masc, curvy, fat, or even tall. You can adjust tit size. You can't make yourself or even your favorite singer.  You can make Harley Quinn. Oh. And you can give her a big or small penis. Hahahaha. She has a dong now.

There's really no roleplaying in the game either. There is one right answer to all dialog options and no responsiveness to different choices. Your V is just  not really customizable.

But,  I hear you arguing, you never really see your character in the game (you know, other than the times you see them naked or vulnerable), so why does it matter?  It matters in that I'm really not sure why they bothered. It's clear that the point of having female characters in this game is so the male player can leer at them, but you can't even play in 3rd person and stare at V's ass.  If there's no roleplaying and no flexibility on the character creator, why spend the resources on it at all?  Why not let people upload a bitmap portrait like in the old CRPGs? The game's resurrection from its first release through Phantom Liberty is well documented. A bug filled failure, victim of greed and crunches. But instead of walking away with their tail firmly between their legs, CDPR took the complaints and criticisms to heart, and began a long-term renovation. By patch 1.61, the game actually was playable and you didn't wait for the inevitable crash. With patch 2.0, they rewrote everything from skill trees to fundamental game play. Phantom Liberty may be the only DLC released for the game, but it's one of the best, period. 

The game is based on Mike Pondsmith's TTRPG, and the influence of that game is all over the DNA of 2077. CDPR made changes to fit a video game better, but the fundamental story of living in a world under corporate oppression, the wealthy beyond the law's reach, and survival meaning sometimes giving up on your dreams, remains. The graphics, five years later, are still a benchmark. The story and the characters will draw you in, and your choices often make more of a difference than you think.

A lot of time has passed since launch, and only now can I truly say it: this game is a masterpiece. The work CD Projekt Red put into turning this around is fantastic.

The plot tackles real, massive issues reflecting our own world. This isn't just a brief main quest that feels like a small add-on to a massive map—it’s a deeply human story filled with heroes, villains, and losers. It asks what it really takes for a "nobody" to become a legend, and more importantly, what price you pay for that success. This is pure, authentic Cyberpunk. To be honest, I wasn't sure CDPR could pull it off, but the voice acting and performances are fabulous. They brought Night City to life so convincingly that you instantly buy into its ruthless rules and struggles.

Gameplay at launch was okay, but weak. Today? It’s phenomenal. The world is packed with hidden details, easter eggs, and its own urban legends. As for bugs, I rarely ran into anything major—just the occasional floating car or clipping geometry. For where the game stands today, it plays great. It just needs a few tiny polish tweaks, but nothing that ruins the experience.

The map is huge, and the DLC filled in every empty space seamlessly. There are countless small stories to uncover and interesting places to explore. The level design and world-building deserve serious praise.

Summary:
Without spoiling anything: trust me, you won't regret playing this. It’s far from a typical video game story—it’s something much deeper. Accept the rules of Night City, jump in, and experience it. The writing and acting ensure this world never feels like a hollow cardboard set; the city is cruel, and you will feel every bit of it.

If you love playing DnD for an equal mix of roleplay and optimizing for combat, and you have a decent idea of how DnD works you'll be set to know what you're doing in building a character and playing in turn based combat. If not, there is a learning curve at the top of the game, you're going to have a lot of options thrown at you and it's a lot to learn all at once. On the other hand as well if you are expecting an exact 1:1 replica of 5e tabletop play, you'll probably be grumpy too, but if you can accept that they had to jigsaw 5e rules to work in a video game because they can't possibly account for every single subclass, spell, or feat the way you can on table top then you'll learn to love the off center replica of DnD.
All of the romances have different weights, but you don't HAVE to romance any of the characters if you don't want. Your decisions do actually effect the way your companions view you as well, so not everyone will take an interest in your character, some may be antagonistic towards you, but it is possible to keep everyone pleasant with you without too much going out of your way. That being said there is also lots of replay ability, you can zig zag all over the place with choices, explore different paths, go wild with it. If you're set on one specific way of things going, you're going to have to save scum a lot, but it's not impossible to get your ideal outcome.
Of course the voice acting is amazing, the writing is excellent and varied, the locations are stunning, the story arc is great, so on so forth.

My only complaint is the multiplayer is a little janky. Ran into so many glitches playing with friends that I never have in my solo runs. Save often if you play with friends over distance so you can reload as needed.

Other than that, I love the game top to bottom, I will still be playing this decades from now I am sure.

- The decisions you make, and the story itself is very malleable and impressively adaptive.

- Inventory management is not fun.

After Dark Souls III introduced me to the Souls formula, Elden Ring felt like the natural next step and apparently all those hours spent learning to "git gud" actually paid off.

I had very similar feelings about Elden Ring to the ones I had about DS3, although this time around I found the experience somewhat easier. Not because the game doesn't have its fair share of difficult bosses and encounters, but because I already knew what these games expected from me. DS3 had taught me to be patient, learn attack patterns, adapt and try again rather than immediately panic when something wanted to murder me.

And yes, I'm still a magic user. Some things never change. 😅

The move to an open world worked beautifully for me. There's an enormous amount to explore, and discovering completely new areas while simply wandering around the Lands Between was one of my favourite parts of the experience.

The Eternal Cities were easily my favourite locations. Nokron and Nokstella have such a beautiful, otherworldly atmosphere that discovering them for the first time really stuck with me.

My favourite boss, though, has to be Rennala, Queen of the Full Moon. Maybe there's a slight magical bias there... 🌙

I enjoyed the story and lore as well. Like Dark Souls, Elden Ring gives you a world where there's always more beneath the surface if you're willing to look for it, and piecing everything together is part of the experience.

The soundtrack is fantastic too, especially some of the boss themes and, as seems to be becoming a tradition with games I love, several tracks inevitably ended up on my Spotify playlists.

Shadow of the Erdtree was also a great addition and gave me another reason to return to a world I'd already spent so much time exploring.

Dark Souls III taught me how to "git gud". Elden Ring gave me an enormous world in which to put that lesson to use.

And, naturally, I did most of it by throwing magic at things from a safe distance. 🧙‍♂️✨

Hear ye, hear ye, Lords and Ladies of the Competitive Realm!

Counter-Strike 2 is a battlefield worthy of legends. A game of steel nerves, cunning strategies, and glorious headshots. Here, friendships are forged in fire, rivalries are born in blood, and every round is a tale worthy of the bards. The thrill of clutching a 1v5 is sweeter than victory at the Iron Throne, and the sound of an AWP firing is music to the ears of even the coldest lord of Westeros.

The skins? Oh, what a splendid treasury! From crimson blades worthy of House Lannister to dragon-lore rifles fit for the Targaryens, one may adorn their arsenal in magnificent fashion. For in this realm, it is not merely how you slay your foes, but how gloriously you do so.

The competition is fierce, the stakes are high, and when both teams are evenly matched, the battles are glorious. Every smoke is a scheme, every flash a deception, and every defuse a race against the Stranger himself.

BUT LO, A DARKNESS GATHERS BEYOND THE WALL.

For this realm is plagued by a most vile affliction: the poison of cheaters.

Wallhackers, who see through stone as if blessed by the Three-Eyed Raven. Aimbotters, whose arrows never miss, whose bullets find skulls with the certainty of a prophecy. Suspicious lords who turn corners with knowledge no mortal ought to possess. They roam the servers like White Walkers, corrupting the living and extinguishing the joy of honest warriors.

And what of the honourable player who trains for countless hours, perfects their aim, studies the maps, and fights with all the skill they possess? They are left wondering whether they were bested by a better warrior or struck down by some foul sorcery beyond the laws of the realm.

'Tis a cruel fate, to enter the arena seeking glory, only to discover that the enemy has brought a dragon to a knife fight.

Still, when the stars align, the teams are fair, and the cheaters are banished beyond the Wall, Counter-Strike 2 remains a magnificent contest of skill, teamwork, and nerve.

My verdict, therefore, is this:

A glorious game with the heart of a champion, the soul of a warrior, and the potential to rule the Seven Kingdoms of competitive shooters.

Yet its throne is besmirched by treachery, and its kingdom weakened by those who forsake honour for hollow victories.

Valve, the realm cries out for justice! Sharpen thy anti-cheat, strengthen the Watch, and cast these foul sorcerers into the frozen wastes!

For a kingdom cannot thrive when its honest warriors grow weary of fighting shadows.

Would I recommend it? Aye.

But I would sooner trust a Lannister with my gold than trust every death replay in this cursed realm.

As someone who has put over 1600 mods into Skyrim, this feels like a heavily modded version of TW3, not a true remaster. I know they already did a next-gen update, so they had to call this something different, but calling it a remaster was a mistake. It does not live up to the expectations that word sets.

This remaster has stripped away a lot of the magic by desaturating the color and making everything look more realistic. The original game looks like a beautiful painting. This game looks like an unreal tech demo where they think higher quality bushes and realistic lighting constitutes better art direction. It doesn't.

The lighting changes/additions are not well executed at all. Putting aside the complete loss of the original's brilliant color grading and art direction, ray tracing and path tracing look decent outdoors. However indoors is a different story. Ray tracing sometimes works indoors, but path tracing almost never works indoors. Half the huts in White Orchard are pitch black indoors, including ones with quest NPCs. I had to keep switching between PT and RT and raster to try and get the least bad lighting for the moment. Not best lighting, least bad. 

Menus are weirdly laggy and glitchy, and somehow the fps seems lower in them even those steam tells me I'm getting 100+ frames. Again, how did that get missed? 

Geralt attacks non-existent enemies instead of the one right in front of him. I'm sure that was a problem in the original game, but for a remaster that supposedly fixing the combat issues...they are still there, unfixed. 

After nearly completing White Orchard, I think I'm just going to roll back and play the original version of the game, or maybe the next-gen. From what I've researched it's generally more faithful to the original vision.

A beautiful, open-world Souls Like that most will probably enjoy, especially if they are new to the genre. Technically it's the entry with the most new gameplay mechanics and stunning graphics as well as amount of bosses and areas to explore/clear out, however, aside from that it doesn't have much else better from previous titles.

I played through DS2 and all the DLCs as well as NG+, it's my only experience with the series but it was a really good one. So when I entered the world of Elden Ring I had similar expectations of the bosses and enemies and general ideea of exploration, except they couldn't be applied. ER takes such a inbetween position of gameplay that it utterly annoys me how disrespectful it is to the player, it tries to stay on two stools, one which is Dark Soul's movement/dodge based wait out with punishment to the boss after their combo, and to the Sekiro's/Bloodborne aggressiveness of the enemies/the player...? 

Most notably the only real mobility change the player gets in combat is jumping, which would have been a nice addition if it wasn't for how ridiculously inertialess it feels. Finding the actual gap where you can attack the enemies and bosses freely or at least even just trade with them - is extremely tiring. The recovery time for the combo's are so short your gameplay will be 95% of the time just seeing someone's body and a bunch of metal sounds and bright flashes while constantly spamming dodge. Dark Souls at least had you use your actual positioning/walking/running and not just dodge rolling at the correct time so you had  a more balanced type of gameplay between the boss and yourself.

Horseback fighting is also extremely clunky and unsatisfying, most enemies that were designed around it are really not entertaining to fight against because they are so much easier when using the horse. It should have stayed as a mode of transportation since the springstream mechanic is quite fun and the world is already pretty big. To continue - the world being big doesnt necessarily mean it's shallow as a puddle, but I would have definetely preffered if they condensed the world by 2x and not made the curious player feel like they waste time 90% of the time. Dark Souls while linear would always reward curious players, so when i came over to ER and started looking over each nook and cranny only to get useless crafting materials - well it's just discouraging and feels like the developer trying to take out as much time out of you as possible.

Ashes of War are perhaps the only good mechanic that came out of this entry and even then from the little use that I did have with them, it seems most are extremely niche and likely to never be used in favor of other objectively better ones leaving 90% of them to never be used and be clutter. Take this with a grain of salt as I didn't use them all that much.

Overall, while the game is good and many new players will enjoy it - I wouldn't buy it if you are self respecting Dark Souls fan. The game caters rather hardly to the hardcore players and I say this as a DS2 fan which had the same allegations thrown against it. Elden Ring is through and through made to break your patience and test just how much are you ready to adapt to it's bosses and new mechanics constantly. God forbid you are a UGS user in this game, good-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥-luck, you will need it.

Granted I have not yet finished the game yet, I cannot bring myself to do so, it feels like im forcing myself to play this game. But I still do have (I think) enough playtime to form some sort of opinion based on what I have played. From the bosses and enemies I have had to fight, none of them were difficult, and most only took 1-2 tries. I know there are probably harder enemies and bosses in the rest of the base game, and DLC (from what ive heard) but thats not the main problem I have with this game. I do plan on eventually completing the game and DLC, but until I do that my review will stay as is and I doubt it will change. 

The main issue I have with this game is that for most of my time playing its straight up riding on horseback going from one castle or cave to the next while having to fight pathetically easy ass enemies in between. At first it was really cool riding a horse and exploring the world, but eventually it got boring and tedious. I know one of my compliments was that there were things to discover and explore, and that is true, once you found a new castle or cave or whatever to get into THAT was fun, but for the other majority of the game, you are just left riding on a horse until you get to those fun parts, and even then they don't last very long sadly. Maybe I just prefer the more "linear" (I don't think Dark Souls 1 is linear) Dark Souls games, but for most of the time, it never felt dull, repetitive, or felt like I was simply waiting for there to be a fun moment like I do with this game. I get its an open world game, but its still. The reason I don't have this issue with RDR or RDR2 is because the combat while on your horse in those games is actually fun, and there's more you can do with your companion, even having a bonding level with the horse and various other mechanics. I think they dropped the ball not making the 1 animal your around for 99% of the game have more mechanics than just feeding them when they have low HP. 

Another thing is that at least for me there was almost nothing rememberable about this game compared to the other ones. I can think of several moments, enemies, characters, etc... from the other souls games, sekiro, bloodborne, that have stuck with me off the top of my head. The only cool thing I can remember is when you are about to fight Radahn you can see other characters in the game at the Castle ready to be summoned and fight alongside you. As far as im aware its the first time you could summon this many people and it felt very cinematic and cool. Again, something really cool that happens because its a main boss / castle. Another L for the rest of the open world area. I just find it extremely funny that even though its an open world game, the best parts is when you aren't in the open world, like in a castle, cave, etc... 

I think this game would have benefited from being not open world, or at the very least having a smaller world. Again, I do plan to finish this game eventually, and change my review accordingly, but until then all I can say is that as a game itself it is fun somewhat, but compared to the other Souls games or From Soft games, its the weakest one. 

I do expect alot of criticism / hate and I suppose theres nothing I can do about that, but these are just my opinions and if you enjoyed the game I'm happy that you did.

Highly Rated, But a Tedious and Punishing Trial-and-Error Experience
Rating: Not Recommended
If you are buying this game based on its glowing masterwork reviews, hoping for a smooth and immersive fantasy RPG adventure to relax with after work, you should think twice.
1. Extremely Vague and Frustrating Mission Guidance
The quest design offers little to no clear directional guidance. Instead of rewarding exploration, the system leaves you to blindly fumble around huge maps. This lack of structure leads to aimless wandering rather than any real sense of discovery.
2. Punishing Invisible Traps and Chain-Aggro Mechanics
What is often praised as "unrivaled freedom" is actually a hyper-fussy physical and rule simulator. Simply walking over to inspect an area can trigger beast aggression, call over guards, and sound alarm drums—instantly turning an entire encampment hostile and forcing a GAME OVER. A single misstep can wipe out tens of minutes or hours of progress, creating immense frustration.
3. Tedious Micro-Management and Fractured Combat
The combination of mandatory turn-based combat and complex D&D rules makes every action feel like solving a math problem. Party members frequently unlink or get stuck behind terrain, requiring constant, tedious micromanagement. The combat lacks fluid feedback and feels more like administrative homework than rewarding gameplay.
Summary:
This game may appeal to hardcore players who have endless free time to study tabletop rulebooks and enjoy trial-and-error reloading. However, for players seeking a fluid, enjoyable fantasy adventure with direct positive feedback, playing this is simply an exercise in frustration.

"haha d*ck implants malfunction" vibes. The characters are all caricatures, stereotypes, blown to the extremes. Voice lines sometimes feel like they recorded them out of order over several sessions with no cohesion or flow. You are constantly being slammed by messages and calls and side information but there really isn't that much reason to read it all because there's very little substance to the world building and it feels tedious. It also doesn't feel like you actually change the course of the game at all as often your dialog options are the same but just worded differently. 

If we look at gameplay: the main missions offer a bunch of ways to get the objective done. That's cool. Outside of that there's no dialog options to talk your way out of things. Stealth is not really rewarded and a lot of it is just combat. I think the framework for this game is solid. The art direction is very cool. The music is solid. The factions and stuff that's all good. There really doesn't seem to be any other approach you can take. My first character was a street kid, and I made him Black, inspired by one of the hairstyles. But there's only one male voice, and it's a dirtbag white voice, and it didn't fit the character at all. So I immediately restarted and created a female corporate character. The voice fit, but the prologue quest suggested a double-cross choice that I wanted to take but wasn't permitted to, after which the game thrusts the player into a bleak introductory mission that's pretty much entirely on rails. A training sequence suggests that nonlethal takedowns are a thing, but then the game basically tells you that they're a bad idea and that you should just kill everybody. I was hoping for Neuromancer, but it felt more like Grand Theft Auto.

Also, despite the fact that my character was supposed to have superb reflexes, I couldn't make the dodge controls work. I'm a piano player; if I can't press the right keys at the right time, that is not a well-designed key sequence. In short, it was shaping up to be a grim, frustrating experience that didn't allow me the kinds of choices I wanted to make and had been taught by other games to expect that I could make, so I bailed out and requested a refund. I guess I'll never learn whether or not it deserves the hype, because I wasn't excited by anything that happened in my first two hours of play.

If I could give a mixed recommendation, I would, including for Liberty City.
Summary for folks who want the brief - the main game plot is supposed to be a ticking time bomb where the MC have a limited time to save themselves, despite the worldbuilding and the core gameplay design contradicting it.
That's it, now for a more critical reflection below.

Unlike previous Witcher projects, the main storyline is relatively quick (20-30 hours). For people who defends the game with all the side quests and Phantom Liberty DLC, the gameplay doesn't reflect the ticking time bomb. There is no timer for quests, and since you are somewhat expected to reach multiple endings by playing through branching side quests, you actually lose the plot and momentum by doing everything else.

Imagine if you play Red Dead 2, but on the last arc - you feel like something is missing if you didn't experience the freedom and glorious adventures in the previous arcs. CPK have this issue, and it's terribly rushed with some characters' arc being noticably trimmed down. You either have to forgo the mentality of a ticking time bomb, or you get the worst and more unrewarding main story content if you choose to focus on it.

I play main as female V because she, like Kassandra from AC: Odyssey, have the better VA. V's background honestly feels underwhelming and only affects some of the choices you will make, like getting more money. For a corpo, she doesn't feel like it, and the decision to age her down from 28 to 23 does affect your believability of her. 
The game also over-balanced itself after patch 1.6, removing many fun previous mechanics like shooting through walls, hacking through walls, putting silencers on other guns besides pistols, and more customizability. Now, it kinda forces you to balance your character and build, which isn't as fun.

Everything else besides the main plot, including the characters, world, and combat, are all very fun. It is basically the Witcher gameplay with sci-fi elements. You can feel the project is rushed before the scope of their destination is reached, and I love the world so much I feel like it ruins part of the experience for me.
Hell, I'd argue the overbalanced nature of later patches was because the overall game, including sidequests, are maybe 80-100 hours in total content and it isn't nearly enough to have a bigger and more complex skill tree.

I also gave it a bad review because, like many cultured players, the decision to not add romance for both Aurore and So Mi cripples me for days and I had to install mods to regain small parts of my sanity. Despite this game promising a lot, the romance and a few quests felt short of, well, being short. There is something amazing here if they choose to tap into more, and I hope their Orion project sequel will deliver.

Some settings also don't do what they say they do. For instance, changing the preset on DLSS to any other setting does absolutely nothing. Turning DLSS off altogether literally turns EVERYTHING into extremely blocky textures.  DLSS is supposed to decrease your image quality in favor of AI upscaling and some more FPS. Here, you absolutely need to keep it turned on just to keep your game looking like it at least belongs in the 21st century. That is NOT what DLSS is supposed to do.

Aside from that, the game runs smoothly on 1440p and all max settings for me (with DLSS turned on for reasons stated above), but for some reason, I have absolutely MASSIVE input delay (2 to 3 seconds) despite my frame latency being relatively low (< 50 ms at all times). No matter what settings I change, the input delay stays the same. This isn't a frame latency issue, it's a game issue, and it makes the game completely unplayable. So yeah, I couldn't even tell you what updates they made to the actual game mechanics because the absolute fundamentals of the game are already so hopelessly broken to begin with.

Slightly hypocritical review, as I have enjoyed The Witcher 3 in the Next-Gen version, and I still will after downgrading from the Remastered version to Next-Gen with DX11 (Next-Gen and Classic are still available under the Beta branches).

But what CD Project Red and the gaming industry as a whole is doing with these graphical "upgrades" is madness.

I have spent hours tweaking the graphical settings for the game to look as good as it did in the Next-Gen update while maintaining solid 60 FPS, with mixed results. I can get it to run on 1440p@60 FPS with ultra/high settings and no Ray Tracing, but the problem is that it doesn't look good [i]consistently[/i].

This is because they have somehow introduced dynamic color pallets and lighting, so that the colors and illumination changes in different areas. Sometimes interiors are dark, sometimes a very bright gray. Sometimes it switches between looking good or bad as the colors and lighting changes from one frame to the other.

On top of that there are a tons of graphical glitches, popping, broken distant models, shadows, etc. And worst of all constant crashes, but I believe that this is a Linux/Proton issue that will be eventually fixed.

The "old" Next-Gen version in DX11 runs super super smooth and consistent with lots of headroom with my hardware. And it looks absolutely gorgeous!

What also shocks me is how many official reviews praise the update for the Path Tracing. I'm happy for everyone owning a 1.5k+ GPU, and Ray/Path Tracing are fascinating technologies, but personally think that the price of the hardware doesn't remotely justify these "enhancements". And it would be completely fine to have the options present in the game, but the fact that a 11 year old game becomes so badly optimized for modern mid-end hardware even with all the high-end stuff turned off is not acceptable!

Also some users do run the game with RT/PT, but then heavily rely on upscaling and frame generation. It surely is a matter of taste, but I find the looks too blurry with heavy upscaling and the delay too "floaty" with frame generation. And as I said before, I'm not even a fan of the new color palette/lighting, even with Path Tracing enabled. Summarized, the industry introduces super demanding graphical features to justify insanely expensive hardware, while introducing other technologies to downgrade the image/delay but boost the perceived FPS. And then they slap it onto old games, preventing them to run properly on modern, mid-range hardware.

As for the other new Remastered features, I will miss some of them. I especially like the additional accessibility features and quest markers on the map. Other than that I didn't notice the other improvements much.

I hope the Remastered version gets a lot more polish and optimization when the new DLC drops, so I can jump back into it and hopefully have a decent experience with a mid-range rig.

I've since dropped this game but I would appreciate it if someone would read through this and tell me where i may have gone wrong. Genuine advice would be appreciated. I want to like this game.

Consistency is not really something that you are going to find much of in this game. Its weird to talk about because often times these inconsistencies are intentional like the combat RNG (although intentional does not mean its good). What I want to focus on here in this review however is the consistency of the roleplaying aspect of the game and why I dont think its very good. What really irks me about this game is how said inconsistency in certain places does not translate well to the roleplaying aspect and general content of the game, if you want an RPG that respects your intent in a well polished and consistent manner, this is ABSOLUTELY not it despite the appearance it gives off of being able to do things however you possibly could want. One example of this that is not exclusive and in fact is the largest sign I personally found of a broader issue not just limited to combat in this game is the ability to fight people and cause chaos constantly. You can fight whoever you want and the game allows it and even encourages it as an intended and described approach during certain sidequests, however a good portion of the time, if you want to fight people, you will get curbstomped, and thus might have to rethink your approach and do something you didnt want to do for an outcome you didnt want. My issue is not born of difficulty, its born of the idea that if you want to be a hyper-aggressive gremlin, you are going to be punished for it a lot instead of rewarded and it can make it feel as if certain roleplaying options are not viable (again, not exclusive to fighting everyone), although being "rewarded" in this game is quite a subjective thing for many people. For a game as broad and inclusive towards literally everything as this, it really does not do a good job at integrating every possible way for players to go about things in an equal manner. In fact this exact thing is exactly what made me drop the game at the nere fight in act 1. I prepared as much as I possibly could think I could've, stabbed certain enemies in the back multiple times and save scummed in order to get optimal rolls on the damage values, and still couldnt get past the fight despite wanting to take the route of killing everyone and nere himself in that fight. Its wide as an ocean (everything you can do) but deep as a lake (the polish and value of each approach to a given situation). I dont expect every approach to be equally easy or equally rewarding, but I do expect the game to treat each playstyle it explicitly describes or offers as an equally viable and intentional way to play the game based on its presentation and it just does not manage that in my opinion. On a personal note: I am 35 hours in on one save slot and I have yet to figure out why people love this game so much, but I certainly know that at least for me, this game's unholy amounts of inconsistency in its combat, its tone, its outcomes and the inconsistency in the "RP" in "RPG" is just not for me. If you value roleplaying consistency and viability of your intentions in games, this is not what you are going to find here. Unless you've played D&D a lot in which case I can't really comment because I don't play D&D

They ain't lowerin' prices. They don't care.

DISCLAIMER:
The game is definitely worth buying if you can get it at a massive discount, as in: single-digit price, being that one cannot deny that it is not a complete miss after the massive overhaul and fixes which polished what they could from the infamous initial version.

PROS:
The game obviously had a AAA budget and a fairly long story.
Someone poured their love for the Cyberpunk lore into the concepts and the pre-release marketing promised to deliver it.
If you want to end up with a mindless time-skip in the form of a semi-idle walk-and-click in your Library, this is a good choice. But again: only and only at a massive discount.

CONS:
1. Before anything else, the first thing that destroys the fun in this are the *unskippable* segments.
[spoiler] After Chapter 1 , you are thrown into an unskippable walking simulator with horrendous overeasy gameplay, that suffocates you with hopes of ending every time there is a fade-to-black, but no! At several points you have to literaly press the forward button several times to (!)crawl forward [/spoiler].
And the dialogue skip option is intentionally taken away at instances where you just sit and look at a character the developers deemed to be so important that you cannot skip.
Do you have choices? None that affect the gameplay.

And this can eat up to 15+ minutes of your life at several instances.

2. The gameplay is a an enormous tease and a letdown. You grow powerful incredibly fast and are given such a vast array of ways to combat that I had stopped upgrading my character a tad bit into chapter 2 because I couldn't find a reason to. The enemy AI is atrociously bad and unchallenging, the weapon classes are a gimmick (one even removes the need to aim at all, scoring instant headshots at a click of a mouse) and at first I thought the driving physics were some sort of an in-game joke.

3. The "cyberpunk" starts and ends with cosmetics in an illogical world that is simply any GTA-like space of copy-paste design, but you get to have a universal remote in your eyes.
The characters are unbelievable and the dialogues are cringe-inducing, with propaganda and forced perspectives infused with varying subtlety.

4. The game-breaking bugs that made it infamous are largely removed, but still present. At certain points the loading screen will shut down the game, there are untested spaces where you can get trapped and have to reload, the physics quirks are still present although rare, etc.

I really wanted to like the game and read online review promising the gameplay to get better as time progresses, but even this much time invested in it later, I cannot say that it is a win.
Unless, I repeat, you are to get it at a *large* discount.

[h1]Baldur’s Gate 3 Review – The Horniest Camp in Faerûn[/h1]

Baldur’s Gate 3 is, from a technical standpoint, an achievement.
Full performance capture, cinematic dialogue, seamless co-op, and a level of polish most RPGs never reach. It feels like the new benchmark.

And the combat deserves the praise.
This is the best turn-based DnD implementation ever made. Encounters reward planning. Builds, rolls, and positioning matter. It finally feels like tabletop logic translated into a digital space without losing depth.

If this review were only about systems, it would end here on a high note.

[h2]The Story That Never Dares[/h2]

The problem is the narrative.

For a game this large and this celebrated, the story plays it remarkably safe. The structure is familiar, the twists are visible from miles away, and the moral conflicts rarely force you into uncomfortable territory. It wants to be epic, but it avoids being unsettling. It gestures toward boldness without fully committing to it.

The villains suffer most from this caution.

[spoiler]Ketheric Thorm is framed as a tragic, god-touched warlord whose presence should reshape the world around him. Instead, much of his impact is delivered through exposition and brooding speeches before culminating in a fairly conventional boss encounter. The supposed avatar of dread ends up feeling like a raid boss with a tragic backstory rather than a transformative force in the narrative.[/spoiler]

The scale is large. The risk is not.

[h2]Companions Built for Applause[/h2]

The companions are memorable, but often in a performative way. They are designed to stand out immediately. Big personalities. Strong aesthetics.

Yet over time, some arcs begin to feel predictable. Shadowheart’s internal conflict repeats familiar beats for long stretches. Astarion’s trauma-laced charm oscillates between vulnerability and theatrical sarcasm in ways that feel engineered for reaction rather than discovery. They are not shallow characters.

But they often feel curated for engagement rather than organically unfolding.

[h2]The Horniest Camp in Faerûn[/h2]

And then we arrive at camp. The emotional center of the story. The place where bonds should deepen naturally over shared struggle.

Instead, it often feels like the Forgotten Realms’ most efficient speed-dating retreat.

The world is on the brink of annihilation. You have a mind flayer tadpole in your skull. Gods are scheming. Empires are shaking. And somehow, within what feels like a long weekend, half your party is ready to discuss eternal devotion.

It stops feeling like chemistry and starts feeling like a triggered dialogue tree. Intimacy accelerates at a pace that undermines tension. Emotional payoff is replaced by availability. The result is tonal whiplash. Apocalypse outside the tent. Romance queue inside it.

[h2]An Ending That Should Have Roared[/h2]

After dozens of hours, the finale arrives with competence but not with weight. It resolves threads, it ties off arcs, but it rarely challenges the player in a way that feels transformative. For a narrative centered around identity, manipulation, and cosmic stakes, the conclusion feels restrained.

[h2]Buyer’s Regret Verdict[/h2]

Baldur’s Gate 3 is mechanically outstanding and technically industry-leading. As a systems-driven RPG, it deserves recognition. As a DnD combat experience, it sets a standard.

But story and companion writing undermine the atmosphere it tries to build. The ambition in presentation is not matched by ambition in narrative risk.

- The worst enemy in the game is the camera itself. One of the worst if not the worst camera I've experienced.
- The main story is uninteresting at best.
- I like when player is being introduced to a world that lives by itself, having it's own rules, logic, factions etc. In BG3 the world revolves around the player. You're the best, the finest, the strongest, your allies are demigods and EVERYONE wants to f**k you eventually, whether you've romanced the NPC or not. Cyberpunk 2077 might be the first game I've played where I genuinely enjoy the characters, world, story and combat while simultaneously wanting to launch the entire installation into the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sun.

The vanilla character customization is embarrassingly shallow for a game whose entire setting revolves around modifying the human body. Night City is full of people with cybernetic limbs, mechanical jaws, artificial skin, exposed hardware and insane body modifications. Meanwhile V gets some lines on his face and apparently we're supposed to go, “Yep, I'm a cyborg now.”

So naturally, I went to mods.

That was a mistake.

Want cybernetic arms? Great. Download the arms.

Except you also need a framework.

And another framework.

And a cyberware core.

And an equipment system.

And an Atelier system.

Then you launch the game and discover the store exists BUT THE ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ARMS AREN'T IN IT because apparently you downloaded the framework for the arms, the store for the arms, the system for equipping the arms, and everything else required to contemplate the philosophical concept of an arm — except the actual ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ arm.

Quit game. Nexus. Download. Vortex. Deploy. Launch game.

Now there are six stores.

Four are empty.

WHY ARE THEY THERE?

Install more mods to populate them.

Quit game. Nexus. Download. Vortex. Deploy. Launch game.

Want gauges? Same ♥♥♥♥.

Want facial cyberware? Same ♥♥♥♥.

Want clothes that don't look like V dressed himself by blindly sprinting through a futuristic Goodwill? Welcome back to Nexus.

And God help you if you install a giant mod collection hoping somebody else has already assembled all this into a coherent package. I tried that. I ended up with 300+ mods, stores containing nothing, stores containing nothing but shoes, mountains of Fem V cosmetics I couldn't use, dependencies for mods I didn't want, and absolutely no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ idea which piece of this Jenga tower was responsible for what.

I eventually deleted the collection and discovered I'd spent more time modding Cyberpunk than playing Cyberpunk.

The frustrating part is that underneath all this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, I actually like the game. I care about these characters. Panam is fantastic. Night City is incredible. When the combat and cyberware fantasy clicks, it's awesome.

That's precisely why this pisses me off so much.

A game called CYBERPUNK should not require an undergraduate degree in ArchiveXL, TweakXL, RED4ext, redscript, Codeware, Equipment-EX, CET, Virtual Atelier and whatever other technological incantation I've forgotten just so my character can LOOK LIKE A ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ CYBORG.

The modding community has produced some genuinely incredible work, and individual mod authors clearly put enormous effort into it. But the user experience of the Cyberpunk modding ecosystem is atrocious. Dependencies stacked on dependencies, content separated across downloads, storefronts separated from merchandise, inconsistent installation methods, and documentation that frequently assumes you already understand the ecosystem.

After hours of troubleshooting, installing, uninstalling, launching, quitting, relaunching and wondering why another ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ store is empty, I have reached enlightenment:

Maybe the real cyberpsychosis was the mods we installed along the way.

10/10 Panam.

9/10 Night City.

2/10 character customization.

0/10 second job as an unpaid Night City systems administrator.

I played this game way back when it was first released on PC, I played it on the PS4, and I played it on PC twice in the last 4 years. Great game then.

The remaster, on the other hand, is a ridiculous and degenerative experience. Anyone coming fresh to this, and only ever playing this version, will probably hate the experience.

In 4 hours I have seen the following:

*) Graphics glitches that are inconsistent even as glitches. Sometimes the exact same region or screen will glitch out in an entirely variant way. Consistently though, the colours vary, the water glows so bright you cannot bear it for long, and the grass will suddenly turn black. But not consistently. Sometimes it'll be fine. 

*) Gameplay is...broken. Variously broken. Again, not consistently. For the first hour it was fine, and today it is not. With no gameplay settings changes between the two play sessions, it has gone from so-so combat to getting one-shotted by pretty much everything that isn't a human being. Strangely, I'm invincible against humans. But a wolf? Nah. One bite...Geralt dead.

*) Cutscenes are...odd. The colour saturation changes dramatically, and everyone looks greyish/brown. As well, now, but not during the first session, when in conversation there is a persistent thrumming sound that is so loud it can drown out nuances in dialogue.

*) Combat is another kettle of drowners. But not a good one. The new features (are there any?) seem not to exist. Unless one of the features is that none of the applied skills apply. It could be a choice, I suppose, but maybe not. Maybe yet another bug. As well, HUD artefacts sometimes just disappear, but luckily your health doesn't matter anyhow, since that one-shot thing is a thing.

I could probably go on, but nah. The thing is, this is an old game that was refreshed and made much, much less playable. Unlike all the folks who can't even get it to run, it does run for me...and that makes it worse, because I got to see (sometimes), hear (sometimes), and feel (way too much) how broken it seems to be.

What I will say is that despite the problems some folks claim are hardware related, I have much more demanding games running very well, so one would think that the team who developed this would have tested it better. But then maybe during testing there were so many graphical glitches they couldn't see what might be broken.

Until the bugs are fixed, there is no way I would recommend this to anyone. 

And...to the studio, this does not bode well for the DLC that is coming, or the Witcher 4. If the former is built on this disastrous foundation, good luck; and if the latter is as buggy as a remaster of a perfectly serviceable old game, the launch is doomed. It won't make any difference how pretty it is, if it is unplayable.

It was a major disappointment for me. While on paper this game has everything that it needs to be crowned as a masterpiece DLC, and while the first impression upon entering into the DLC provides further merit to that sentiment, very quickly does it fall on its face. 

We have seen this before? This is just an extension of the vanilla late game. Sure a ton of weapons, a ton of bosses and enemies, but at this stage of the game its a bit redundant unless you are ready to reset your character. Its fine to do that but ultimately its just a different path up the same trajectory. 

This vast DLC is... largely empty. It feels like a copy-paste of the altus plateau with slightly darker shades. 

The story, same as in the vanilla, seems very irrelevant. And while this is a staple of From Soft Souls game, in ER it is getting a bit too tiring and not cohesive considering the scale of the game. 

The bosses are the worst offenders. While I'll be the first to admit that I am not a speed/challenge runner, I played all the previous games and enjoyed them vastly. Struggled, sure. But still the bosses were enjoyable. In Shadow of the Erdtree, and ER by and large, the bosses seem without vision or balance. From the peaks of Sekiro and DS3, to bosses here that simply spam attacks, are too large to properly track and read, and generally contain levels of unprecedented bull...  

I wanted to like this DLC and the game. I even gave it a long break, upgraded to fully modern hardware, and watched a bunch of videos about how to properly implement jumping, strafing, and unlocking the camera to better move around bosses and enemies. But putting aside the fact that I am not the best player, the game had failed for me at the simplest level. It had failed to be FUN. Trudging through ER late game and the DLC is a slog. And while the vistas are astonishing... the content and the mechanics fall far, far behind.

Is it a recommendation? Sure, on a technical level it is still a masterpiece that needs to be experienced. The scale of it (while also its downside) is alone a cause for celebration. But a more polished experience with better executed ideas lies in DS3 and Sekiro.

Elden Ring is the rare open-world game that actually earns its size. The map is huge, but almost every corner has something worth finding - a dungeon, a boss, a weapon, or just a view - and the game never holds your hand toward any of it.

Combat is the usual FromSoftware loop of learning attack patterns and not getting greedy, but the open world and spirit ashes make it more flexible than previous Souls games. You can brute-force a fight, come back later, or summon help. The bosses are the highlight: memorable, hard, and usually fair once you stop panic-rolling.

Build variety is excellent. Strength, magic, faith, and hybrid setups all work, and the weapon types keep things interesting past the first 20 hours. Performance is solid on a decent PC, though the occasional stutter still shows up.

It is long, sometimes opaque, and the late-game difficulty spike is real. If you like figuring things out yourself and don’t mind dying a lot, it’s one of the best games of its kind. About 130 hours in and I’m still finding new stuff.

This is my third attempt to get into this game. I'm done.

I want to love it. I've played the previous Baldur's Gate titles, I enjoy the genre, and I'm not looking for hand-holding. What I do want is a narrative that gives me a reason to care about what I'm doing next.

BG3 mistakes "mysterious" for "unclear." There's a brain worm in my head that's supposed to be turning me into a monster — that's a genuinely compelling hook — but the game keeps forgetting to remind me that's the point. I'm following quest markers because the markers exist, not because the story is pulling me forward.

The world is reactive and beautifully constructed. The writing is sharp when it wants to be. But the moment-to-moment narrative momentum is weak. Conversations can collapse into combat without warning. The game withholds information under the guise of tension when it's actually just poor player communication. There's a difference between a mystery that feels earned and one that leaves you genuinely confused about basic decisions.

Three attempts. Uninstalled. The brain worm wins.

This remaster is a disaster. Whoever greenlit its release instead of delaying it seriously needs to be fired. 

I own The Witcher 3 on Steam, PS5, GOG, and Xbox Series X, and I've now tried the remaster across multiple platforms.

On PS5 and Series X, it's essentially unplayable for me. There's constant stuttering while riding Roach and during nearly every combat encounter I've experienced so far. It's a miserable experience, and I won't be playing either console version again until CDPR releases a patch addressing the performance issues. Then there's PC.

Before the remaster, I could comfortably average 90–100 FPS on Ultra settings. After the update, I'm lucky if I can reliably maintain 45–50 FPS. That's an enormous performance hit. Also, the dialogue audio is far too quiet compared to the rest of the mix and I'm constantly having to adjust the volume just to hear characters speaking. 

I've also encountered more bugs in roughly two hours with the remaster than I remember encountering throughout my previous Witcher 3 playthroughs.

This update should have been delayed. There's no good reason it needed to release in this state. I understand that it's a free update, and I appreciate that, but being free doesn't excuse releasing a buggy, poorly optimized remaster with the expectation that the problems can simply be fixed later.

I loved the original Witcher 3, which makes this even more disappointing. But based on my experience across PC, PS5, and Series X, I cannot recommend the remastered version in its current state. Until CDPR addresses the severe performance problems, stuttering, and visual bugs, I'd stay away.

The way to describe Baldur's Gate 3 would be that the game is very, very wide, but also incredibly shallow. And I honestly think if Larian had about half the budget and actually thought about what to do with the game, it could have been a lot better.

Now, let me expand on why "I can't stand the graphics."
Overall I despise most games that are trying to do photorealistic graphics, in 99% of cases it looks disgusting to me. Good graphics don't need to be anime or cartoony or some kind of vivid spectacle. But if you want photorealistic graphics I would heavily consider stylizing them around something, or make the graphics just insanely good. 
Like Alan wake 2 is photorealistic, but it puts insanely high focus on environments and it's very noisy in its presentation, plus it's horror and very high fidelity, so it looks good. Which is probably another point, remedy uses real actors and the characters looks not just photorealistic but real. Which most games fail to do and the fake photorealism is inherently wrong. 
That's a stance on graphic design I will die on. Almost every AAA game puts emphasis on graphics and pretty much all of them fail miserably. 

Animation in baldurs gate 3 is something you can't defend, it's utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Characters simply stand in place and talk, in a very rigid pose with almost no emotion. And then when they need to move they suddenly get into an animation that is incredibly choppy and then they go back to standing and talking. There is absolutely no fluidity or movement to it, no emotion behind character actions. 
Even the scene where if you play a bard you get to do a whole song, while the song itself is pretty nice and the narrative around it is actually kinda cool, watching your character do that song is taking you out of it. Which again, photorealistic graphics with very rigid 3d models is the fault at bad animation. 

Which also ties to character creation, where you can't complain much about DND choices, it's copying a system and the system itself is by my standard terrible. But the visual creation is bad... Which is still connected to graphics, but it's insanely difficult to make a character that looks pretty and there are no sliders or anything, there's like 8 preset faces and most of them are ugly as ♥♥♥♥. 
Hair selection is probably the only good thing there. And it's cool you can look at your ♥♥♥♥ but overall the game doesn't really do much with nudity anyway. If you give me an option to have a dangling penis between my legs then have a decency of letting me use it as well xD 
But another thing, some people will see a lot of races and subraces. They are all humans. Human with pointy ears. Short human with a beard. Even gith are just humans with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up faces. The only non humanoid option is dragonborn and the only reason it is an option is because larian already have lizard models from original sin. 
The beauty of playing a fantasy game is playing nonhuman fantasy races. The very least we could have gotten was tabaxi. But their photorealistic graphics don't allow for individuality. 

Everyone is edgy wasn't exactly the criticism, I didn't really specify it, so that's on me. But the criticism would be "overly edgy". You can have good edgy characters. But bg3 companions are incredibly shallow and one noted. 
I keep hearing they get a lot better and deeper once you get far enough and explore the dialogue options but that's not something I'm willing to discover. Wasting 30+ hours on finding out that the character is not an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is too much time. 
You can write mysterious and intriguing characters without making them obnoxious. 

Combat is something I didn't enjoy in original sin as well, and it's practically the same here. It is deceptively complex. You can in theory spend a lot of time optimizing and strategizing but in the end it's all just dice rng that can heavily make or break the entire combat. On higher difficulty it could be different and all, but it's not a type of game to play for difficult combat, the story and characters are the main drawing point, so playing on normal or even lower is fair. 
And there the combat just slogs through because you're given a lot of options for very little value, often to your own detriment actually when just clicking an enemy for normal attack is gonna do a lot more than anything else. And it just slogs in round after round. 
You might say that pathfinder is even worse but that's not true because pathfinder has that granular strategy that can heavily change outcomes of combats. Plus pathfinder does have real time with pause so you can fast forward through trash fights while focusing more tactically in turned based on boss fights. It's stupidly difficult and often also boiled down to ♥♥♥♥♥♥ dice rng. But it is a lot more complex and rewarding because of it. 
Slog doesn't mean it takes long, just that the amount of time taken is not satisfying. And BG3 combat is not satisfying in any way.

This is a very difficult review for me and I cannot show all my motivations in this section, after all if you are reading this you want a quick opinion before you buy the game.

First of all, I’m sure that most of this reviews here are from genuinely honest people that enjoyed this game, and I can see why. The mechanics are impressive, the implementation of powers, spells, skills it’s a breath of innovation; for the most part the game feels alive with interaction of NPC, great voice acting, choices and consequences. 
If this game was called something like “Legends of Forgotten Realms” or “Heroes of the Sword Coast” and wasn’t connected in any way from the previous Baldur’s Gate saga I would love this game 100%.
But sadly it is not.

The fact is, in my opinion, Baldur’s Gate 2 Throne of Bhaal was the perfect ending for the saga, maybe a little rushed  (the developers they were hurrying due to the upcoming shutting down of the company).
A book also from those years established the canon ending, clearly stating the fate of most of the notable characters, even the Bhaal Spawn.
I played dozens of time BG and BG2 plus the expansions, I shared those moments with the community of the time and we appreciate the character’s arch and stories of each one. 

 Then Wizard of the Coast released the modules Descent to Avernus and Murder in Baldur’s Gate, compromising the endings from the awesome series by reintroducing PNG that were supposed to be elsewhere or not existing. 
And probably Larian’s writers did even worst, [spoiler]by no respecting the few good canonic elements and reconnecting the main plot to the previous BG chapters.[/spoiler] 
All because they want to grab more income by squeezing a well loved brand that most people out there do not remember so well anymore. 
Larian had the resource  to write an all new story, a new brand for a spectacular title. Instead they lacked courage by playing safe.
Also I want to mention the impressive presence of bugs related to sub quest, graphical errors that breaks the immersion  especially in the last chapter of the game. Considering the game was in early access for a very long time (full price around 60 bucks) and the use of AI during the last period of develop this is a very reprehensible conduct. 
I do not reported the bugs and errors I encountered during my experience.

My only hope is in the newer generation of player. Who may enjoy good stories, who may discover the first games and who wants to appreciate the old adventures and perfect ending… do not stop on the surface and find out how the game industry was different back then. 

I know we are not so many anymore and maybe this message is not important; but if YOU are like me, a real fan of BG, do not buy this game. It’s an insult to all the original BG’s writers and the gamers who loved the series.

For anyone considering buying the Witcher 3 now and playing it on PC, unless you have a literal data center at your disposal than wait a while because the performance might hurt your experience of what is for many the single best title ever made.

Elden Ring is genuinely one of the best games I've ever played.

The exploration is incredible. You can pick a direction, wander off, and somehow end up finding an entire castle, underground city, or boss that you had absolutely no idea existed. The combat is satisfying, the build variety is ridiculous, and the feeling of finally beating a boss that's been kicking your ass for an hour is something very few games can replicate.

It's not perfect. Some bosses can be frustrating as hell, the PC performance has had its issues, and occasionally the game seems determined to remind you that you are, in fact, terrible at it.

But overall? Elden Ring is an incredible game and absolutely deserves the praise it gets.

Unfortunately, the Tarnished Pack is where FromSoftware and Bandai Namco completely lost me.

$5 for two starting classes, a handful of armor and weapons, some NPC invasions, and three cosmetic skins for Torrent is already pushing it. But the fact that some of the equipment can be obtained in-game anyway makes charging for this feel even more ridiculous.

And then they bundle this content with the new Switch 2 version while turning around and telling the people who already bought and supported the game on other platforms to pay extra for it.

Seriously?

This isn't a real expansion. This isn't Shadow of the Erdtree. Shadow of the Erdtree gave us an entire new world to explore, bosses, weapons, enemies, and dozens of hours of content. That was DLC worth paying for.

The Tarnished Pack feels like they looked at a small amount of bonus content that could have been a free update and decided, "Nah, let's charge them for it."

And before someone says, "It's only $5," I genuinely do not care. The price does not magically make bad DLC practices okay. If anything, it's the principle of it. Elden Ring has sold millions of copies. People have supported this game for years, bought Shadow of the Erdtree, and helped make it one of the biggest games of the last decade.

So rewarding those players by making them pay extra for a couple of starting classes and horse cosmetics while giving the content to new Switch 2 buyers as part of their edition is just insulting.

I still love Elden Ring. The actual game is phenomenal.

But I'm not going to pretend the Tarnished Pack isn't a blatant attempt to squeeze more money out of an already massively successful game.

This is perhaps the hardest review I have ever had to write, because I literally have to recommend against playing what I think is a great game, but I cannot, because it is marred by a thick buggy web that prevents my enjoyment of it.

So first off, the game does have some great characters, excellent musical score, an interesting world / plot, and an overwhelming amount of choices you can make so that no 2 playthroughs are alike. The writing can be a bit weak / contrived at times, but this is a D&D high fantasy game, it comes with the territory.

The game is split into 3 acts, and Act 1 is absolutely brilliant. It's a slow burn that really gives you time to warm up to the gameplay and learn how the combat works, but it doesn't hold you hand so much that it hampers that feeling of natural exploration and discovery. My how I loved act I.

Then comes Act II.... and well, the game starts to break down. Plots resolve incorrectly, progression doesn't work randomly for some quests, enemy AI kept breaking. The nonsense just kept piling up, but I was having a good enough time I could ignore most of it.

Then Act III, which is larger than Act 1 and 2 combined. It's a disaster, SO MANY quest bugs. SO MANY issues with the enemy AI. Things that worked ok in Act 1 and 2 are just broken here. My characters would glitch through doors randomly, when I issued commands in combat, the character would start to take the action, nothing would happen, then I lose my action. Jumping is just all out broken, my characters would freeze in mid air then would make the death falling noise and I would take damage. Enemies would freeze in combat and do nothing for a full 10+ seconds, EVERY. SINGLE, ROUND, making it a nightmare of a slog to get through a single combat. I would often focus down enemies simply because their AI was bugging out and I just couldn't standing watching them sit their and drool while doing nothing again.

I can put up with A LOT for a good game, but no matter how good BG3 is otherwise, it's just to much to bear. The game seems to be getting worse with each patch, which is mind boggling. This game needs to be rebuilt from the ground up in a working engine, because this is just not a good experience as is. I honestly don't think most of the people reviewing this game well made it through Act 3, because there is no way you can ignore this many issues.

Maybe the game works better on consoles, that could be worth looking into as it's a real shame to miss out on such a good narrative experience, especially since this is perhaps the most epic D&D based game ever released. I really wish the studio that made it had let it cook longer, but oh well, not much we can do now.

Deck runs at about a constant 85-90C, so there's small room for graphical improvements, but none that would matter for stability or performance. This is what I consider unplayable. I can spend hours upon hours upon hours upon hours dedicated to improving my aim, learning the map, discovering new strategies and playing the game as it is supposed to be played – only for someone with a fresh account and a cheat to come into my lobby and turn it into a glorified target practice. I will report them, receive my prize of an empty “report received” message and pray that the next match won’t be another round of Hackerman Simulator 2026.
But what’s worse is that cheating in this game – and the lack of anti-cheat measures – destroy the game from the inside. The very premise of a competitive FPS is ruined when it’s possible to simply install a better cheat. Why would players invest time and money into the game if they can simply “download miracle cheat 3.0” and become the best player in the world?
The developers could have solved this problem in the past, but instead, they give us empty speeches about “community reports” and “dedicated servers”, giving us the same tired answers over and over again:
Hackers appear → players complain → devs promise action → nothing meaningful changes → hackers come back.
 It’s not funny anymore. The competitive FPS genre revolves around trust – and this single fact has been understood by cheat creators from day one. This development team, however, apparently does not have a brain, and that is a serious problem. The enemy team isn’t even the problem.At this point, the hackers aren’t cheating – they’re testing the quality of the anti-cheat and the dedication of the developers. Good gunplay, potentially fun gameplay, ruined by the feeling that I am playing the game against not opponents, but an army of script Kiddies who enjoy cheating. Baldur's Gate 3, while decent, is extremely overhyped and underwhelming.
Having played both Baldur's Gate 1 and 2 to death, and loving every moment of it, I was severely disappointed in how they handled its nominal successor.

Where BG1 and BG2 gave a long, intricate, story-rich adventures that felt like they spanned a full country's worth of areas, BG3 offers three and a half areas (the Underdark area of part 1) with a small bit of story, and a few sidequests here and there. 

It also comes with its fair share of annoyances, such as:
-Not being able to pause, ever, citing "you don't need to!" as their reason (it's usually true, but absolutely not 100% so).
-When engaged in conversation with a person or an object, it's *always* the character initiating the conversation (on purpose or by accident) that does the skill check, regardless of how (un)realistic it would be for them to do so (here they could have learned a ton from the creators of the Pathfinder games)
-Time only being counted through long rests makes the game less immersive
-Inventory handling is a mess
-Being able to teleport items to your camp is unimmersive
-Being able to teleport to and from your camp at will (outside combat) is unimmersive
-Movement in combat is buggier than it should be
-Several instances of mechanics or effects are mentioned and never explained, leaving it as an exercise to the reader to attempt to work out what they do (i.e. google it, and hope to avoid spoilers in the process - they show up in the dumbest places)
-Only four party members at a time leaves less room for party dynamics and "on-the-fly" story
-Almost all party members are highly good-aligned, leaving you with almost no choices if you want an evil-aligned campaign with members that have a story

In sum:
BG3 is far smaller, shorter and less engaging than the originals, and only does one thing better than them: Graphics and voice acting, which seems to be where they put 70% of their time and effort, despite this being a *roleplaying game*. If you like RPGs, play all the other good ones before you bother with this one (on sale).

Where do I even start with Baldur's Gate 3?

I've been playing D&D since I was around 11, so there was absolutely no way I was going to miss this game. I hadn't played the previous Baldur's Gate games, though, so BG3 was actually my introduction to the series. I got it as soon as it became available, and almost 1,000 hours later... apparently I'm still not done with it.

Achievements aren't really the focus for me here. I'm currently at 46/54, but BG3 is one of those games where I'd much rather start another character, try another choice and see where the story takes me than worry about completing a checklist.

The amount of freedom and variation is probably what I love most. Even after so many playthroughs, different interactions, consequences and unexpected outcomes can still appear. You make one seemingly insignificant choice differently and suddenly you're seeing something you've never seen before. It makes every run feel like its own D&D campaign rather than simply replaying the same story.

The modding possibilities make that experience even better. I love that the game can be modded so easily, although I've mostly kept mine to quality-of-life and graphical improvements. For me, it's about polishing and improving the experience without changing what makes the original game so good.

All three acts have something I love, although Act 2 is definitely my favourite. The atmosphere, the story and everything surrounding the Shadow-Cursed Lands just work incredibly well for me.

I love the companions too, although Gale, Astarion and Shadowheart have a special place among them. Gale takes first place when it comes to romance, though. ❤️

As for my own characters, Wizard is easily my favourite class and Drow my favourite race. Character creation gives you plenty to play around with, and combined with all the classes, subclasses, races, backgrounds, dialogue options and different ways of approaching situations, the replayability is enormous.

The story itself is great, but what really makes it special to me is how much it feels like *your* story. My most memorable Tav will probably always be my very first one, whom I played essentially as myself.

That adventure ended in Act 2 because I made a... let's call it a "wrong" decision.

The soundtrack deserves a mention as well. There are some beautiful tracks in there, and naturally, a few of them have found their way onto my Spotify playlists.

My main disappointment is knowing that development was, in some ways, rushed towards the end and that a number of things had to be cut. There are places where you can wonder what BG3 might have looked like if everything originally envisioned had made it into the finished game.

But even with that disappointment, what we got is still far more than excellent.

After 979.5 hours, countless characters, different decisions, romances, successes, catastrophes and apparently the occasional accidental premature ending, I'm still finding reasons to return to Baldur's Gate 3.

And I'm definitely not finished yet.

Now this can be fixed with a mod and the game is still great otherwise, but I could never recommend a game that requires a mod to feel playable.
