If you've never played a Dark Souls, Demon's Souls, or even Bloodborne, starting here is okay. I recommend this game to anyone who has never played a FromSoftware game before. But if you've already played their previous games AND you're hoping to encounter something new, sadly, this is not the case.

The game literally recycles animations, items, attacks, enemies, and mechanics from its past games. Same animations, same attacks, same items, all with subtle reworks to item images and slightly different animations, but underneath, it's the same. I played the previous FromSoftware games and liked them, but I can't ignore that this feels like the same game.

In fact, this game could be called Dark Souls 4, and I'd be okay with it, because that's what it is: Dark Souls with mods.

Btw, I know Demon's Souls came first, but the same lineage is there: Demon's Souls, Bloodborne, Dark Souls, and now Elden Ring. The only game that really escaped this pattern is Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, which actually changed things.

If you look at FromSoftware's games over time, you can see a pattern. They take what they already did, adjust it, and try to perfect the formula, but they don't create enough new things. Look at Armored Core and Frame Gride, for example. It's the same idea, trying to perfect the formula, and then they continue with Armored Core and Another Century's Episode.

I don't care if they reuse elements from past games, but do you know who does this too? Activision with Call of Duty.

And look, Elden Ring is fun, but there are a lot of things that feel like Bandai Namco the publisher, not the developer put its hands on parts of the game. I remember playing Code Vein, the typical Souls like that tries to be unique but ends up feeling like, "Hey, look, I'm Dark Souls too." It was disappointing, with its vague story and some parts like The Depths: Tower of Trials, where the enemy damage made no sense.

Elden Ring also starts with static images instead of the kind of cinematics that gave context at the beginning of Dark Souls, Sekiro, or Bloodborne. I remember thinking, "Wow, wait a second." There are things in Elden Ring that feel like they were just written into the script because yes.

The Fire Giant is a good example. You're close to the end of the game, there is no cinematic and barely any context, and when you reach him, the fight doesn't feel special. Remember Dark Souls III and Yhorm the Giant? If you did Siegward of Catarina's quest, he appeared there, and suddenly the fight had more context and feeling. It felt like you had to finish something.

In Elden Ring, the Fire Giant feels like a boss placed there just to fill an empty, soulless scenario.

The game also has too many bosses. You enter a cave, explore for a while, suddenly a health bar appears, "epic" music starts, and you fight another boss. Then you do it again. Because it happens so often, bosses stop feeling special.

Even the main bosses were a disappointing experience for me. There is so much recycling. Look at Margit, the Fell Omen. I saw that guy like three times, or maybe it was Morgott, the Omen King, because they all look the same. Down in Leyndell, Royal Capital, there is also an illusion that is basically a copy of Margit or Morgott. Even Godrick the Grafted didn't feel that unique to me.

Radahn was also disappointing. Only in the DLC do you really see his power. I understand that the version we fight in the base game is weakened, but still, we're fighting this legendary warrior while he's riding a skinny, scrawny horse.

Malenia, however, actually felt special. She was fun. And the final Marika/Radagon encounter was cool because it felt like the game was telling me, "I'm the Elden Ring." Not me saying it the boss itself felt like it was saying that.

Godfrey was also disappointing. I expected a real version of the Elden Lord, something like when you fight Gwyn or even the Soul of Cinder. Not because I wanted a harder fight, but because of the feeling you get when you fight them for the first time. Godfrey didn't give me that feeling. He felt weak.

And then there is co-op. I bought this game expecting to play with friends, but if you want to play with friends, forget it or at least, that's how it felt to me. You get invaded constantly, and it becomes annoying when you're just trying to explore.

In past games, invasions had a purpose. You could farm items for the covenant you joined and get special rewards, like Darkmoon Blade from the Blade of the Darkmoon. In Elden Ring, that doesn't exist in the same way. Invading other players often feels like PvP for no reason.

And you already have THREE different arenas for PvP. Some people prefer invading because they enjoy it, and that's fine, but from my experience, getting invaded while trying to explore with friends made no sense.

So don't expect to easily play through the whole game with friends. I ended up playing almost the entire game alone, even though I bought it expecting to play with them, and eventually they just left the game because of things like this.

I'm also worried about the direction FromSoftware is taking. This "new DLC" attitude of "it's just $5" makes me worry that in the future the company could become like Activision, Bethesda, or Ubisoft. I really hope that never happens.

And then you see the new FromSoftware game coming to Nintendo Switch another Souls game, or basically Bloodborne with jumps. Do you see the pattern? The direction they're taking? Maybe I'm wrong. I hope I am.

So, who is Elden Ring for?

If you've never played a FromSoftware game: play it. It's fun, huge, challenging, and has an incredible amount of content.

If you've already played their previous games and you want more of the same formula, you'll probably like it.

But if you've played them all and you're hoping to find something genuinely new, think about it before buying. Maybe you won't care that it's the same formula. Maybe you'll love it anyway. But maybe, like me, you'll regret the purchase.

When I watched the trailers and gameplay, I had this feeling in the back of my head saying, "Hey, this is the same game as the past FromSoftware games." And literally, it was.

I wasn't wrong.

A great D&D adaptation, but a frustrating game

Baldur’s Gate 3 does an impressive job of translating D&D rules into a video game. Character classes, spells, abilities, dice rolls and many other mechanics are remarkably well implemented.

Unfortunately, I increasingly dislike the actual game built around those mechanics.

The biggest problem is the combat design. Especially in Act 3, major encounters constantly introduce enemies with special abilities that are poorly explained or completely unexpected. Enemies become invisible, stun characters, move without provoking opportunity attacks, apply multiple status effects, create darkness, and use combinations of actions that are difficult to understand from the player's perspective.

The problem isn't difficulty. **The problem is a lack of information.**

A good D&D encounter gives you enough information to make tactical decisions. BG3 too often makes you discover the rules by getting hit by them first. Eventually combat starts feeling less like *“How do I outsmart these enemies?”* and more like *“What ridiculous special ability did the game just pull out of nowhere?”*

Large encounters are another problem. Watching 15–20 enemies take their turns one after another makes fights incredibly slow. Combine that with all the status effects, animations and special abilities, and some battles become an exhausting exercise in waiting.

The camp system also becomes increasingly annoying. Wanting to take a long rest can turn into another cutscene, companion conversation, romance scene, dream sequence or even a fight. The companions are interesting, but the game sometimes feels like **group therapy with occasional adventuring in between**.

Loot has the opposite problem. In BG1 and BG2, finding a magical item was exciting. In Act 3 of BG3, I constantly find supposedly powerful items and think: *“What am I supposed to do with this?”* Many are so build-specific that they immediately become vendor trash.

And then there are the technical and UI problems: unclear mechanics, missing or misleading indicators, awkward camera behavior, and situations where the game behaves differently from what its descriptions suggest.

I actually like the D&D rules in BG3 a lot.

**It's the game built around them that increasingly frustrates me.**

I enjoyed BG1, BG2, Icewind Dale and Neverwinter Nights much more. They had fewer systems, smaller encounters and less spectacle, but they generally **let me play instead of constantly getting in my way**.

At this point, I frequently find myself asking:

**“How do I beat this?”**

followed by:

**“Do I really want to spend another hour doing this?”**

That's a disappointing place for a Baldur's Gate game to leave me.

**Excellent D&D implementation. Increasingly frustrating game design.**
